kzz7yh-f124844-d1e103.summary: Announces two questions on the third principal topic, the necessity of obedience.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e112.summary: First question: whether subjects must obey temporal lords in paying newly imposed tallages that serve only the lords' temporal advantage.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e121.summary: Second question: whether religious are more bound to obey their spiritual father, the prelate, than their natural father.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e130.summary: First argument that Christians must pay such tallages: Romans 13 commands every soul to be subject to higher powers, and per Aristotle's Topics what is said without qualification is said simply; so obedience is owed in all things.
claims: Subjection to higher powers is unqualified (argument).

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e152.summary: Second argument: 1 Peter 2 commands servants to be subject to masters, not only good ones but also harsh ones; so subjects must obey however burdened.
claims: Obedience is owed even to harsh masters (argument).

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e163.summary: Third argument: Ephesians 6 commands servants to obey earthly masters as Christ, and Christ must be obeyed in all things.
claims: Masters must be obeyed as Christ, in everything (argument).

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e172.summary: Contrary argument from the gloss on Matthew 17 ('the sons are free'): if sons of a kingdom are free in it, much more are sons of the kingdom over all kingdoms free in every earthly kingdom; so Christians need obey temporal lords in nothing.
claims: Christians, as sons of the heavenly kingdom, are free of temporal obligations (argument).

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e189.summary: Second contrary argument: James 1 calls the Christian law the law of perfect liberty, which would be false if Christians had to obey temporal lords.
claims: The law of perfect liberty frees from temporal obedience (argument).

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e205.summary: Third contrary argument: Christians are freed from the Mosaic law, which was divine; a fortiori from human law. Then Richard's solution. Because of our corruption we are prone to disturb justice, so there must be holders of spiritual power under one principal head and holders of temporal power; subjects must obey them within the scope of their power but not beyond, except to avoid scandal. On new tallages he distinguishes. Slaves simply speaking may be taxed even for the lord's benefit, since slave and goods are the lord's property (Aristotle, Politics I). Free subjects ruled politically cannot be newly taxed by lesser lords, especially without royal consent, as canon law forbidding new tolls and censuses shows.
claims: Temporal and spiritual powers exist to preserve justice in a corrupt humanity.
Obedience is owed only within the limits of a ruler's power, except to avoid scandal.
Slaves and their goods are the lord's property and may be taxed at will.
Lesser lords may not impose new taxes on free subjects, especially without royal consent.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e299.summary: Adds Roman-law support: Codex titles forbidding the institution of new vectigalia, and the Digest on laws.
claims: Roman law forbids instituting new levies.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e306.summary: If the lord is a king or prince, he may by his own authority impose new tallages on free subjects for the common good, in proportion to their means and to the nature and size of the need, but only if the resources already assigned to him for the common good are insufficient. If the tallages serve the common good in no way, neither king nor prince may impose them on free subjects, whose possessions are not the lord's, and subjects need not obey because the ruler exceeds his power.
claims: Kings may levy new taxes for the common good when ordinary revenues are insufficient, proportionate to need and means.
Taxes not serving the common good exceed royal authority and need not be obeyed.
The goods of free subjects are not the ruler's property.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e335.summary: Reply to Romans 13: it applies when higher powers keep within their power, which they exceed when taxing free subjects only for their own benefit.
claims: Romans 13 presupposes rulers acting within their authority.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e351.summary: Reply to 1 Peter 2: it concerns slaves strictly, or if it means politically ruled subjects, it is limited as Romans 13 was.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e361.summary: Reply to Ephesians 6: 'as' (sicut) marks similarity, not equality, as in 'love your neighbor as yourself', where one must love oneself more; so we obey temporal lords in all things within their power, as we obey Christ in all things.
claims: 'Sicut' in Ephesians 6 signifies likeness, not equality.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e385.summary: Since the contrary arguments appear to prove Christians owe temporal lords no obedience at all, they too must be answered.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e394.summary: Reply to the gloss on 'the sons are free': it calls sons of the kingdom those Christians who have given up all temporal goods for Christ, and they indeed are not bound to tributes or temporal exactions.
claims: Those who renounce all temporal goods for Christ are free of tributes.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e407.summary: Reply to James: the Christian law is the law of perfect liberty because it frees from spiritual servitude, the servitude of sin, not from temporal servitude.
claims: Christian liberty is freedom from sin, not from temporal subjection.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e416.summary: Reply to the Mosaic-law argument: the Mosaic law was a prefiguring shadow of the Gospel and is fulfilled in it, so it no longer binds literally; human law relates differently to the Gospel, since it helps toward the Gospel's perfection.
claims: The Mosaic law ceased as figure fulfilled in the Gospel.
Human law assists the perfection of evangelical law.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e442.summary: First argument that religious should obey natural parents more: Colossians 3 tells children to obey parents in all things, and whoever must be obeyed in all things is owed more obedience than anyone else.
claims: Children must obey parents in all things (argument).

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e464.summary: Second argument: one obligated to someone cannot bind himself to another to the first's prejudice; a son is bound by divine command to honor his parents, and obedience is the greatest honor.
claims: Prior obligations cannot be overridden by later vows (argument).

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e477.summary: Third argument from the gloss on Exodus 20: whoever does not obey the parents he can obey fails to honor them; so none must be obeyed as much as parents.
claims: Honoring parents includes obeying them (argument).

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e488.summary: Fourth argument: perfect obedience proceeds from charity, so I should obey more whom I must love more, and I must love my natural father more than my prelate.
claims: Obedience follows the order of charity (argument).

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e500.summary: Fifth argument: one is more bound to obey the source of one's being, nourishment and education, to whom one is subject by nature (Ethics VIII), than one to whom one is subject only by one's own voluntary statute.
claims: Natural subjection outranks voluntary subjection (argument).

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e518.summary: Sixth argument: Christ rebukes transgressing God's command to honor parents for the sake of human tradition (Matthew 15); so no vow or tradition may prejudice that command.
claims: Human traditions cannot override honoring parents (argument).

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e534.summary: Sed contra: we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5), and obeying a prelate is obeying God ('who hears you hears me').
claims: Obeying a prelate is obeying God.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e547.summary: Second sed contra: Bernard (De praecepto et dispensatione) says the Rule urges obedience even to impossible commands of the prelate, trusting in God, which would be irrational unless the prelate were owed most obedience.
claims: The Rule urges obedience even in impossible commands.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e567.summary: Third sed contra: Bernard says commands from God or from a human as God's vicar are to be obeyed with equal reverence when not contrary to God; God must be obeyed more than a natural father, so the prelate also.
claims: A prelate as God's vicar is to be obeyed like God.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e580.summary: Fourth sed contra: as spirit to flesh, so spiritual father to natural father; spirit is to be obeyed more than flesh.
claims: Spiritual paternity outranks carnal paternity (argument).

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e592.summary: Fifth sed contra: Matthew 19 promises a hundredfold to whoever leaves father and mother for Christ's name, which the religious does by preferring the prelate.
claims: Leaving parents for Christ merits reward.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e605.summary: Richard's solution: in matters where children are bound to parents by natural and divine law (contained in 'honor your father and mother'), the professed religious must obey the natural father, in due place and time, rather than a prelate commanding the contrary, since religious profession absolves no one from divine precepts, the counsels serving the more perfect keeping of precepts (Decretum d.30, 'Si qui filii'). In matters where children are not bound by natural or divine law, the religious must obey the prelate more.
claims: Religious profession does not dissolve obligations of natural and divine law to parents.
The evangelical counsels exist for the more perfect observance of the precepts.
Outside natural and divine filial duties, the prelate is to be obeyed more than the parent.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e660.summary: Reply to Colossians: 'in all things' means all things to which children are bound by natural or divine law and, for the professed, with regard to place and time.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e676.summary: The second argument is answered by the body of the question.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e681.summary: The third argument is answered like the first.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e683.summary: Reply to the charity argument: one is not always more bound to obey whom one must love more, unless they have equal authority; parents lack the authority over children in non-obligatory matters that prelates have over subjects.
claims: Obedience follows authority, not merely the order of love.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e700.summary: Reply to the fifth argument: it concerns obedience in matters of natural-law obligation.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e709.summary: Reply to the sixth argument: it concerns obedience in matters of divine-law obligation.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e720.summary: Reply to Acts 5: obeying a prelate is obeying God unless he commands against God or exceeds his power. Bernard says the professed cannot be compelled beyond, or restrained short of, what their profession embraces. A prelate commanding against natural or divine filial duties commands against God and is not to be obeyed.
claims: A prelate's command binds only within the limits of the profession and God's law.
Commands against natural or divine filial obligation are not to be obeyed.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e746.summary: Reply to Bernard on impossible commands: that admonition concerns perfection, not necessity, and would equally apply to a son with respect to divine-law duties to parents.
claims: Obedience to impossible commands is a counsel of perfection, not an obligation.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e755.summary: The third sed contra is answered by the reply to the first.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e760.summary: Reply to the spirit-flesh analogy: its premise is false. Though the soul is created immediately by God, the natural father disposes the matter to receive it, so the whole human depends more on the father than on the prelate; the father is therefore the more principal parent in natural and divine-law matters, and the analogy is ill-founded.
claims: The natural father disposes matter for the soul and so is principal over the whole person.
The spirit-flesh analogy does not map onto prelate and father.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e783.summary: Reply to Matthew 19: leaving parents applies where parents do not need their children's honor, especially when they would draw children away from salvation.
claims: Leaving parents is warranted when they impede salvation or do not need support.

kzz7yh-f124844-d1e794.summary: Alternatively, the text refers to matters in which children are not bound to parents by natural or divine law.

kzz7yh-f124844-Dd1e126.summary: Question 1 sets limits on obedience in taxation. Temporal and spiritual powers exist because fallen humanity tends to disturb justice, and subjects owe obedience within the scope of each power but not beyond, except to avoid scandal. Slaves, being property, may be taxed at the lord's will. Lesser lords may not newly tax free subjects, especially without royal consent, which canon and Roman law support. A king or prince may levy new taxes on free subjects only for the common good, when ordinary revenues fall short, and in proportion to need and means. Taxes solely for the ruler's benefit exceed his authority and need not be paid. Romans 13 and the servant texts presuppose rulers acting within their authority. Christian liberty is freedom from sin, not from temporal subjection, and only those who have renounced temporal goods are exempt from tribute.
claims: Obedience to rulers is bounded by the limits of their authority.
New taxes on free subjects are legitimate only for the common good and in necessity.
The property of free subjects does not belong to the ruler.
Christian liberty does not abolish temporal subjection.

kzz7yh-f124844-Dd1e438.summary: Question 2 weighs the obedience a religious owes the prelate against that owed the natural father. In matters where children are bound to parents by natural and divine law, the duties of the commandment to honor father and mother, the religious must obey the parent, in due place and time, rather than a contrary command of the prelate. Profession absolves no one from divine precepts, since the counsels exist to fulfil the precepts more perfectly. In all other matters the prelate is to be obeyed more. A prelate is obeyed as God only within God's law and the limits of the profession. Obedience follows authority rather than the order of love, and Bernard's admonition about impossible commands is a counsel of perfection.
claims: Natural and divine-law duties to parents survive religious profession.
Otherwise religious owe greater obedience to the prelate.
Prelates' authority is bounded by God's law and the profession.

kzz7yh-f124844.summary: Article 3 of II d.44 sets limits on obedience in two applied questions. On taxation, authority exists to preserve justice among fallen humans and binds only within its scope. Slaves may be taxed at will, but the goods of free subjects are not the ruler's. Lesser lords may not impose new levies, and kings may do so only for the common good when ordinary revenue falls short and in proportion to need, so taxes for the ruler's private benefit need not be paid. Christian liberty is freedom from sin, not from civil subjection. On religious obedience, profession does not cancel natural and divine-law duties to parents, which take precedence over a prelate's contrary command, while in other matters the prelate is to be obeyed more.
claims: Obedience is bounded by the limits of legitimate authority.
New taxes on free subjects require the common good and necessity.
Religious profession does not dissolve natural and divine-law filial duties.
